title: Introduce aggregation harness + dependency upgrades to reduce console hotpath noise
creator: Aisha Tan
description: Background: The console backend aggregation path has accumulated several quick fixes that increase resolver fanout, cause duplicate downstream calls, and make caching fragile. This ticket creates an "aggregation harness": a lightweight middleware layer that coalesces concurrent requests, provides a configurable aggregation policy, and stages a set of dependency upgrades (GraphQL server, Redis client, Node) behind a feature flag so we can measure regressions safely. Goals: 1) Reduce aggregate API fanout and duplicate downstream calls by >=35% on common dashboard queries; 2) Improve p95 latency for console aggregate endpoints by >=20%; 3) Reduce Redis key stampede and CPU churn during bursts; 4) Upgrade critical deps to remove known memory/connection leaks and unlock newer instrumentation for tracing.
acceptance_criteria: Aggregation harness implemented as a middleware module and feature-flagged in console config
End-to-end integration tests exercising coalescing behavior (concurrent identical queries -> single downstream call)
Performance benchmark in staging showing >=20% p95 reduction on targeted endpoints and >=35% reduction in duplicate downstream requests
Dependency upgrades merged behind feature flag: graphql -> 16.x, apollo-server -> 4.x (or internal GraphQL server minor bump), ioredis -> 5.x, node runtime bumped to 20.x in the private build image
No increase in error rate or memory growth in 72h smoke run in staging when harness is enabled
Observability: new metrics emitted (coalesced_requests, coalesce_miss_rate, downstream_call_reduction) and dashboards updated
Graceful rollback via feature flag with zero data migration required
technical_notes: Design: harness lives between HTTP handler and GraphQL execution; it canonicalizes query signatures (operation name + normalized selection set + relevant variables) and maintains an in-flight map with short TTL to coalesce identical concurrent requests

Cache intersection strategy: we will not replace existing Redis prefix cache, but the harness will consult and update a small LRU in-process to short-circuit when safe; on cache miss it will register a single upstream fetch and fan out results to waiters
Backpressure: long-running aggregate requests will be sharded by top-level entity (project/org) to avoid head-of-line blocking for unrelated dashboards
Observability: attach span to coalesced work and emit histogram for wait time behind harness; track dropped or stale responses separately

Dependency trade-offs: upgrading GraphQL/Apollo unlocks query plan improvements and tracing hooks but requires schema-compat checks and resolver signature linting; ioredis v5 uses a newer connection model and needs connection pooling verification
Fallback: harness disabled => current code path unchanged; dependency upgrades gated by feature flag plus runtime compatibility layer that polyfills minor API differences
migration_plan: 1) Merge harness stub behind feature flag; 2) Run canary in staging against synthetic load; 3) Gradually enable for 10% of console traffic while measuring metrics; 4) Apply dependency upgrades in separate PRs but keep feature flag disabled until both harness and deps are validated; 5) Ramp to 100% and run 72h smoke tests before marking Done. If memory/connection regressions are observed, roll back feature flag and debug in parallel.
qa_plan: Create E2E scenarios in the console integration suite that spawn N concurrent identical queries and assert single downstream call and correct responses. Add chaos tests to simulate Redis slowdowns and ensure harness still returns eventual responses. Run perf benchmarks with k6 workload scripts stored in internal drive.
risks: Upgrading core GraphQL server may surface subtle resolver ordering/async differences (risk: medium)
ioredis v5 connection changes could increase ephemeral connections during rollout if pooling isn't tuned (risk: medium-high)
In-process coalescing increases memory for tracking in-flight requests during very high concurrency windows (risk: low-medium)
Incorrect canonicalization of queries could cause cache misses or incorrect coalescing (risk: high if not covered by tests)
